item: The launchers open the browser without the passphrases the server holds
summary: Found by an independent security read of PR #1817. A scripted start that sets OO_DB_PASSPHRASE or OO_KEY_PASSPHRASE hands it to the launcher's environment, and the browser the launcher opened inherited it (launch.sh's xdg-open and open; launch.cmd's start of the already-running opener and of the waiting PowerShell that runs Start-Process), so a browser started by the launcher kept the passphrase in its own environment (/proc/<pid>/environ, a crash report) for as long as it ran, after the app had stopped. launch.sh now starts both openers through env -u for each name in OO_HELD_ENV_VARS (the variable is never touched in the shell, so a readonly one still opens the browser), and launch.cmd clears both names inside setlocal before each start, with the waiting PowerShell's clear undone by its own endlocal so the server still receives them. The list is secret_scrub.HELD_ENV_VARS, and tests/test_launcher_browser_env.py holds both launchers to it; it runs the bash launcher against a fake browser and server that record only whether each name was present (the server gets them, the browser does not, on the fresh-start and already-running paths and for each opener), and reads launch.cmd's order statically. NOT MEASURED: launch.cmd on a real Windows machine; a browser that is already running receives the address over its own IPC and was never started by the launcher, so it never held the launcher's environment. STILL OUTSIDE: the launcher's own processes keep it, the shell itself and its stderr filter (tee and awk, which live as long as the server) as well as the curl health probes, and on Windows the PowerShell that asks whether a server already answers; all but one end with the launcher. The exception is launch.sh's deferred record writer (_oo_rec_defer, R174), a detached subshell that ignores the window's signals and waits for the record lock with no bound, so it can outlive the launcher holding both names; an unset inside it would not help, because a forked subshell keeps the environment block it was born with in /proc/<pid>/environ. Narrowing these is a separate change. Both security reads (two independent reviewers) returned SHIP; the tests were widened after them to catch the common other openers in either launcher (gio open, kde-open, sensible-browser, $BROWSER; start, explorer, rundll32, Start-Process) and to pin launch.cmd's outer setlocal. The terminal panel's own opener is PR #1817's.
